blocks.text: 1.1.1 Recognition of Real and Imaginary Parts
Let us start with the following equation:
\(\sqrt{-1}\) does not belong to the set of real numbers. For convenience we call it an imaginary number and denote it by \(i\) (read as iota).

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Every real number is a complex number with 0 as its imaginary part.

In the complex number \(z = a + ib\), \(a\) is called the real part and \(b\) is called the imaginary part of the complex number. We write \(a = \operatorname{Re} z\) and \(b = \operatorname{Im} z\). For example, if \(z = 3 + 4i\), then \(\operatorname{Re} z = 3\) and \(\operatorname{Im} z = 4\).
The product of a non-zero real number and \(i\) is also an imaginary number and is written as 1. Thus \(2i\), \(-3i\), \(\sqrt{5}\,i\), \(-\frac{11}{2}i\) are all of this kind.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints "and is written as 1". The product of a non-zero real number \(b\) and \(i\) is written as \(bi\) (or \(ib\)), as the examples \(2i\), \(-3i\), \(\sqrt{5}\,i\), \(-\frac{11}{2}i\) show.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The imaginary part is the real number \(b\), not \(ib\). For \(z = 3 + 4i\), \(\operatorname{Im} z = 4\), not \(4i\).
Two special cases:
If \(b = 0\), then \(z = a\) is an ordinary real number (this is the Note above).
If \(a = 0\) and \(b \ne 0\), then \(z = ib\) is called (purely) imaginary, like \(2i\) or \(-3i\).
So the real numbers sit inside \(C\): \(\mathbb{R} \subset C\).

Let \(z = a + ib\) be a complex number. Then \(a - ib\) is called the complex conjugate of \(a + ib\). It is denoted by \(\overline{z}\). Thus \(5 - 4i\) is complex conjugate of \(5 - 4i\) and \(-2 - 3i\) is complex conjugate of \(-2 + 3i\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints "\(5 - 4i\) is complex conjugate of \(5 - 4i\)". Changing the sign of the imaginary part of \(5 - 4i\) gives \(5 + 4i\), so \(5 + 4i\) is the complex conjugate of \(5 - 4i\) (and \(5 - 4i\) is the complex conjugate of \(5 + 4i\)).

blocks.text_alt: if z equals a plus i b, then z bar equals a minus i b

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
To write the conjugate, keep the real part as it is and change only the sign of the imaginary part. Think of it as the mirror image of \(z\) in the real axis (you will see this in the Argand diagram, 1.1.5).
Why is a real number self-conjugate? A real number \(a\) is \(a + 0i\); its conjugate is \(a - 0i = a\), the same number.
Taking the conjugate twice brings you back: \(\overline{\overline{z}} = z\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(i = \sqrt{-1}\) (iota), the imaginary unit.
2. For \(z = a + ib\): \(\operatorname{Re} z = a\) and \(\operatorname{Im} z = b\), both real numbers.
3. Every real number is a complex number with imaginary part 0.
4. \(\overline{a + ib} = a - ib\): only the sign of the imaginary part changes.
5. A real number is its own conjugate.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.text:
Writing \(\operatorname{Im}(3 + 4i) = 4i\). The imaginary part is \(4\).
Changing both signs for the conjugate: \(\overline{3 + 4i} = -3 - 4i\) is wrong; the correct conjugate is \(3 - 4i\).
Forgetting a minus sign: in \(2 - \frac{5}{7}i\), \(\operatorname{Im} z = -\frac{5}{7}\), not \(\frac{5}{7}\).
